name: SV Colo

profile.reading:
SV Colo, styled SVCOLO by the company, traces its roots back to 1994, when it launched as an internet service provider under the name Meer.net. As demand for dedicated hosting space grew during the early 2000s buildout of the commercial internet, the company opened its first colocation facility in Sunnyvale in 2002, then relocated its main operation to Santa Clara in 2004, where it has continued operating since. SV Colo describes itself as owned and managed by its own principals, a privately held, independently run colocation business rather than a subsidiary of a larger data center real estate company or private equity portfolio, a meaningfully different ownership structure from most of the large wholesale and hyperscale operators that have come to dominate the Santa Clara and greater Silicon Valley data center market over the past decade.

On its own site, SV Colo markets a range of services aimed at businesses of varying sizes, from startups to large multinational enterprises. These include colocation by the cabinet or the cage, custom built hosting arrangements, prepackaged service bundles, burstable colocation for variable workloads, and carrier neutral network access allowing customers to choose among multiple internet and network providers rather than being locked into one. The company advertises SSAE 16 Type II audit compliance and PCI compliance, both standard third party assurance frameworks relevant to customers running payment processing or other regulated workloads, along with round the clock on site technical staff and remote hands support.

What SV Colo's public materials do not include is any hard technical specification. There is no published square footage, no stated IT power capacity in kilowatts or megawatts, and no cooling system description. The precise current street address is also not conclusively settled from the sources reviewed here. Reverse geocoding of this facility's recorded coordinates resolves to an unrelated automotive repair business address in Santa Clara, not a data center, so the exact parcel this facility occupies is not confirmed against county property records, even though the company's own history page confirms Santa Clara as its operating base since 2004.

Santa Clara sits at the center of one of the most data center dense counties in the country, and a small, independently owned, three decade old colocation operator like SV Colo represents a different segment of that market than the hyperscale campuses now surrounding it. It is a legacy Silicon Valley hosting business that predates the modern cloud era and has continued serving a customer base of smaller and mid sized businesses even as much of the industry has consolidated around a handful of very large operators.
profile.research_note: Operator site confirms certifications (SSAE 16 Type II, PCI Compliance) and sales/support phone, but no sqft, IT capacity MW, year built, or generator MW is published.

reading:
SV Colo, formally Silicon Valley Colocation Inc, is a small independent colocation provider in Santa Clara, California, and it belongs in this registry as a reminder that the market did not begin with hyperscale campuses. The company tells its own history plainly. It started in 1994 as an internet service provider called Meer.net, leased its first colocation space in Sunnyvale in 2002 once it saw customers wanting cabinets rather than dial up, and moved to its current Santa Clara facility in 2004, where it has stayed. It says it is owned and managed by its principals, which sets it apart from almost every other Santa Clara operator in this registry, where the ownership chain usually runs to a REIT, a private equity fund or an infrastructure vehicle.

What SV Colo sells is straightforward. Cabinets, cages and custom suites, cross connects on a carrier neutral basis, remote hands, environmental and power monitoring, and a hundred per cent uptime commitment on facility systems. It states SSAE 16 Type II and PCI compliance. What it does not publish is almost everything a capacity registry would want. There is no square footage on its site, no utility service figure, no critical IT load, no design density in watts per square foot or kilowatts per cabinet, no generator or uninterruptible power supply rating, and no carrier list. The company directs anyone wanting those numbers to its sales line. This registry therefore records no capacity for SV Colo rather than borrowing an estimate, and readers should treat any capacity number for this operator found elsewhere as unsourced.

The public record that does exist is municipal rather than corporate, and it is about the city rather than this operator. Santa Clara owns its electric utility, Silicon Valley Power, which is the reason so many data centres clustered here. The utility states that Santa Clara hosts more than fifty data centres and that data centres account for about 53 per cent of its power use and sales, and it advertises some of the lowest electricity rates in California, with commercial and industrial rates reported at roughly 36 to 51 per cent below the neighbouring investor owned utility. Reporting on the city's own accounts puts data centres at roughly 13 per cent of general fund revenue, including about 24.6 million dollars of a 37.3 million dollar utility transfer tax in the 2025 to 2026 fiscal year. The city requires new facilities to run on carbon neutral energy under its climate action plan, and 31 existing data centres use recycled water. The constraint now is delivery rather than demand, with Silicon Valley Power committing on the order of 425 million dollars to grid work and with reporting that newly built Silicon Valley capacity has waited on power connections.

None of that is a statement about SV Colo specifically, and this entry does not present it as one. It is the environment a long lived independent operates in, where the scarce input is a substation position rather than floor space, and where a company that took its Santa Clara building in 2004 holds a connection that a new entrant cannot now easily obtain.
